children: U.S. soybean futures closed modestly lower on Thursday after a choppy session while surging cash prices for soymeal, a feed ingredient, underpinned the market, analysts said.

Meanwhile, the run-up to next week's meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping kept attention on Chinese demand for U.S. soy. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that he planned to meet his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng this weekend.
Corn and wheat futures ended lower, consolidating below three-year highs set earlier this month.

Chicago Board of Trade November soybean futures (SX26) settled down 3/4 cent, or 0.06%, at $13.19-3/4 per bushel, staying below last week's contract high of $13.35-1/4. Benchmark CBOT December soymeal (SMZ26) ended up $5.70, or 1.6%, at $371.30 per ton, after reaching $375.60, the highest on a continuous chart of the most-active contract (SMv1) since May 2024.

Supplies of soymeal, a high-protein soybean product used in livestock and poultry rations, have tightened in the U.S. Midwest in recent weeks. Soybean processing plants in the region typically shut for routine seasonal maintenance ahead of the autumn soybean harvest, but this year's downtime appeared to be more extensive than expected, brokers said, limiting production of soymeal and soyoil.
Then, heavy rains stalled the early harvest this week in key states like Iowa, slowing the arrival of soybeans into processing sites.

"Meal is the market of the moment, for sure," said Terry Linn, analyst with Linn & Associates. "I see it being driven by technical buying and a bit of seasonal supply tightening from processor maintenance that ... is forcing users to scramble for coverage," Linn said.
Corn and wheat futures were more subdued, pressured by a sluggish crude oil
market and lingering hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to ease disruptions to Black Sea grain trade.
CBOT December corn (CZ26) ended down 3-3/4 cents, or 0.7%, at $5.30-1/2 a bushel and December wheat (WZ26) fell 3-3/4 cents, or 0.5%, to finish at $7.27 a bushel.

Wheat traders said an AFP report, which cited a Turkish proposal sent to Russia and Ukraine for a truce on strikes against commercial shipping in the Black Sea, put attention back on de-escalation prospects.

However, traders were cautious given that Turkey has already flagged such proposals, while a deal to halt strikes on energy infrastructure announced by U.S. President Trump on Monday had little effect on the ground.
